BSZ panel $106.8B · JR panel −$32.3B

Comparison of the two analyses of California Proposition 40: Overview · Open Output (here) · Open Analysis: Report and Slides · Open Materials Also in this project: BSZ analysis explorer · JR analysis explorer

Why do the two analyses of Proposition 40 disagree?

The BSZ analysis (Boll, Saez and Zucman, August 2026) finds that the billionaire tax raises money for California. The JR analysis (Jaros and Rauh, NBER, September 2026) finds that it loses money. This page puts both on one measure, the net fiscal effect: the wealth tax collected, plus extra income tax from asset sales, minus the income tax lost to people who leave.

BSZ main estimate1 $106.8B Over 5 years: the wealth tax, net of the income tax it adds and loses.
JR main estimate1 −$38.9B Net present value: the wealth tax minus the income tax lost for ever, in today's dollars, averaged over the authors' model runs

Today's dollars (present value): what money received or lost in future years is worth now.

Move the BSZ panel's dials top to bottom, each to its far end: each term is what that dial changes. The Walk the path button in each panel does it for you. The report gives every step.

Two panels, one estimating function

Each slider moves one disputed input from the BSZ value (left end) to the JR value (right end). The BSZ panel starts at the BSZ values, the JR panel at the JR values. Tap or hover over a symbol or an end for what it means.

Notes on the two estimates and the conventions

1 Each analysis's own main estimate, defined its own way. The BSZ analysis's is a net total over 5 years: the wealth tax (Table 5 row 1), plus extra income tax from assets sold to pay it, minus the income tax lost to billionaires who leave, for 5 years at 3%. BSZ's own headline is the wealth tax alone; the net total is this OPA's choice, explained on the BSZ analysis overview. The JR analysis's is a perpetuity net present value, averaged over the authors' Monte Carlo draws (Jaros and Rauh, NBER chapter c15504, Tax Policy and the Economy vol. 41, September 2026).

The net fiscal effect puts both on one definition, and the panels start at its two ends. The BSZ end is $106.8B and the JR end −$32.3B, a gap of $139.0B. Both ends discount the lost income tax at one rate, 3% a year, the rate the BSZ overview uses. The JR analysis's own headline is −$38.9B: the authors draw the discount rate at random between 1.5% and 4.5% and average, which is worth about $6.7B more than one 3% rate.

Conventions. All amounts are nominal billions of dollars. The wealth tax is counted at face value when assessed and undiscounted, as both analyses do (the BSZ analysis values the base on 1 July 2026; the JR analysis grows its 2025 Forbes base by 7% to 31 December 2026). Present values are at the assessment date, at 3% a year. The JR code labels its rate r − g and the text r (the JR analysis's mismatch 3).

Notes and data

Where the numbers come from. Every number on this page is computed by comparison/R/ from the two analyses' export contracts (bsz-analysis/export/r/, rjkdc-analysis/export/r/: the files each pipeline writes for others to read) and the transcriptions in comparison/data/. The estimating function is score_common() in comparison/R/model.R, with a Python twin (R and Python agree to 1e-9 on every exported number; see comparison/tests). The browser runs model.js, a copy of it, and a test runs that copy with node over 600 slider mixes against the R values, to 1e-9. The report derives each number step by step and shows the bridge from the BSZ end to the JR end; the materials page lists the code, tests and files.

Data. ends.csv (the two ends, at each horizon setting), slider_sample.csv (300 slider mixes per panel with their values, the sample the tests run model.js on), inputs.csv (every disputed input and its sources), DISPUTES.md (the crosswalk of the disagreements, one row each, with what each analysis says and where), dial_path.csv (the terms of the equation at the top, dial by dial), comparison-data.js (what this page reads). A test fails if comparison-data.js or this page differs from the generator's output.

Kinds. Each slider's explanation ends with the kind of its two values: data (settled by observable facts), research (a published estimate), guesswork (asserted without data or a study behind it), guesswork on data (a judgement applied to observed facts) and scenario (a choice of which world is estimated). "A vs B" reads the BSZ value's kind against the JR value's.

The function. The report states the estimating function line by line. The left sliders move only the left bar and the right sliders only the right bar.
